title: C# Web APIs: Build a Server
summary: Build the server side of an app with ASP.NET Core: answer HTTP requests with minimal APIs, read route values, query strings and JSON bodies, validate input, organize code with services and controllers, and save data with Entity Framework Core.
objectives: Explain HTTP requests and responses: methods, paths, headers, bodies and status codes
Build endpoints with ASP.NET Core minimal APIs that answer with text, JSON and the right status code
Read route values, query strings and JSON request bodies, and validate what clients send
Organize a server with services, dependency injection and controllers
Save and query data with Entity Framework Core

lessons.title: Your first server
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Your first server

When you open a website or an app, your device sends a message across the internet: *"Please send me the weather"*. A **server** is a program that waits for those messages and answers them.

- The message your device sends is a **request**.
- The server's answer is a **response**.

A server that answers with data (not whole web pages) is called an **API**. Apps, games and websites all ask APIs for things.

### A request has a method and a path

```
GET /weather
```

- **GET** is the *method*: it means "please send me something".
- **/weather** is the *path*: which thing you want.

### Your first server in C#

Here's a whole server. It's real C#: the same code works on a real computer.

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
var app = builder.Build();

app.MapGet("/", () => "Welcome to the Grove!");

app.Run();
```

1. The first two lines **build** the app.
2. `app.MapGet` makes an **endpoint**: *"when someone asks for GET /, run this and send back what it returns"*.
3. `app.Run()` **starts** the server, so it can answer requests. It always goes last.

The part with `() =>` is a little method with no name. Whatever it returns becomes the response.

### Answering with an object

Return text and the server sends text. Return an object, and C# turns it into **JSON** for you, the format almost every API uses:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/weather", () => new { sky = "sunny", temperature = 21 });
```

The response looks like this:

```json
{ "sky": "sunny", "temperature": 21 }
```

### Did it work? Status codes

Every response starts with a number called a **status code**:

- **200 OK**: it worked.
- **404 Not Found**: there's nothing at that path.

Ask this server for `GET /dragons` and it answers **404**, because no endpoint has that path.

### Try it!

Codegrove runs your server right here. Press **Run** to start it, then use **Try it** under the Output panel to send it a request and see the response.

### New words

- **Server**: a program that waits for requests and sends back responses.
- **Request**: a message asking a server for something, like `GET /weather`.
- **Response**: the server's answer: a status code and some data.
- **API** (*Application Programming Interface*): a server that answers with data for other programs to use.
- **Endpoint**: one path the server answers, made with `app.MapGet`.
- **JSON** (*JavaScript Object Notation*): the text format APIs use to send objects, like `{ "sky": "sunny" }`.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A Grove weather server with two endpoints. It doesn't print anything: it waits for requests. Press **Run**, then in **Try it** send `GET /` and then `GET /weather`. Try `GET /dragons` too, and see the **404**.

lessons.title: HTTP and your first endpoint
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## HTTP and your first endpoint

Almost every app you use is split in two: a **client** (the app on your phone, a website in your browser, a game) and a **server** somewhere else that stores the data and does the work. They talk over **HTTP**, by sending **requests** and **responses**. A server built for other programs to call, answering with data instead of web pages, is a **web API**.

### What's in a request

```http
POST /scores HTTP/1.1
Host: api.skyline-racers.test
Content-Type: application/json

{ "player": "ByteRunner", "time": 92.4 }
```

- **Method**: what kind of action. `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `PUT` replaces, `PATCH` changes part of something, `DELETE` removes.
- **Path**: which thing, like `/scores` or `/players/42`. It can end with a **query string**: `/scores?top=10`.
- **Headers**: extra details as `Name: value` lines, like `Content-Type`, the format of the body.
- **Body**: the data being sent, if any. `GET` requests usually have none.

### What's in a response

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Location: /scores/317

{ "id": 317, "player": "ByteRunner", "time": 92.4 }
```

The first line has the **status code**. Its first digit tells you the family:

| Code | Family | Common ones |
|---|---|---|
| 2xx | Success | 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content |
| 3xx | Go somewhere else | 301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified |
| 4xx | The client got something wrong | 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict |
| 5xx | The server failed | 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable |

Clients make decisions from status codes, so picking the right one matters as much as the body.

### A minimal API in ASP.NET Core

**ASP.NET Core** is .NET's framework for web servers. `dotnet new web` gives you this `Program.cs`:

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
var app = builder.Build();

app.MapGet("/", () => "Hello World!");

app.Run();
```

- `WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args)` sets up configuration, logging and **services** (lesson 4).
- `builder.Build()` makes the app.
- `app.MapGet(path, handler)` adds an **endpoint**: requests with that method and path run the **handler**, a lambda whose return value becomes the response. There's `MapPost`, `MapPut`, `MapPatch` and `MapDelete` too.
- `app.Run()` starts the server and **blocks**: it keeps waiting for requests until the server stops, so nothing after it runs.

This style is called **minimal APIs**. Lesson 5 shows the other style, controllers. Web projects import the ASP.NET Core namespaces for you, so there are no `using` lines.

### What the handler returns decides the response

| Handler returns | Status | Content-Type | Body |
|---|---|---|---|
| a `string` | 200 | `text/plain; charset=utf-8` | the text |
| any other object | 200 | `application/json; charset=utf-8` | the object as JSON |
| an `IResult` | you choose | depends | depends |

JSON property names are **camelCase**: a `record Lap(int LapNumber)` comes out as `{ "lapNumber": 1 }`.

When you need a status other than 200, return an `IResult` from the `Results` class:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/leaderboard", () => isEmpty
    ? Results.NoContent()                 // 204, no body
    : Results.Ok(topTen));                // 200 + JSON

app.MapGet("/race", () => Results.Problem(
    "Track closed for repairs.", statusCode: 503));
```

`Results.Problem` sends **problem details**: a standard JSON shape for errors (`application/problem+json`) with `type`, `title`, `status` and `detail`. Clients can show `detail` to the user.

Both branches of a `? :` must have the same type, which is why both sides use `Results.…`: mixing `Results.NoContent()` with a plain `topTen` list won't compile.

### Running it in Codegrove

In a real project, `app.Run()` starts **Kestrel**, ASP.NET Core's web server, on a port like `http://localhost:5000`, and you'd call it with a browser, `curl` or an `.http` file. Here, Codegrove's practice server stands in for Kestrel inside your browser, so press **Run**, then send requests from **Try it**. The C# is exactly what you'd write in a real project. A request that matches no endpoint gets **404**; a path that exists with the wrong method gets **405 Method Not Allowed**.

### New words

- **HTTP** (*Hypertext Transfer Protocol*): the rules clients and servers use to send requests and responses.
- **Web API** (*Application Programming Interface*): a server that other programs call over HTTP, answering with data.
- **Method**: the kind of request: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE.
- **Status code**: the three-digit number at the start of a response that says how it went.
- **Header**: a `Name: value` line with extra details about a request or response.
- **Endpoint**: a method and path the server answers, with the handler that runs.
- **Minimal API**: ASP.NET Core's style of mapping endpoints straight onto the app with `app.MapGet` and friends.
- **Problem details**: the standard JSON format for error responses (`application/problem+json`).

lessons.title: Paths with blanks
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Paths with blanks

Your notice board server answered fixed paths like `/hello`. But a creature guide can't have an endpoint for every creature! Instead, you leave a **blank** in the path, and whatever the visitor types there is handed to your code.

### A blank in the path

```csharp
app.MapGet("/creatures/{name}", (string name) =>
    $"You asked for {name}");
```

The curly braces `{name}` are the blank. It's called a **route value**.

- `GET /creatures/frog` runs the endpoint with `name` set to `"frog"`.
- `GET /creatures/owl` runs it with `name` set to `"owl"`.

The method's parameter must have **the same name** as the blank: `{name}` fills `string name`.

### Found it, or not?

When someone asks for a creature that isn't there, the polite answer is **404 Not Found**. `Results` lets you choose:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/creatures/{name}", (string name) =>
{
    var found = creatures.FirstOrDefault(c => c.Name == name);
    return found is null ? Results.NotFound() : Results.Ok(found);
});
```

- `Results.Ok(found)` sends **200 OK** with the creature as JSON.
- `Results.NotFound()` sends **404 Not Found** with nothing else.

### Only numbers, please

Add `:int` inside the blank and it only matches whole numbers:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/creatures/legs/{count:int}", (int count) =>
    creatures.Where(c => c.Legs == count));
```

`GET /creatures/legs/8` works. `GET /creatures/legs/lots` doesn't match at all, so the server answers **404**. The `:int` part is a **constraint**: a rule the blank has to follow.

### New words

- **Route**: the path pattern an endpoint answers, like `/creatures/{name}`.
- **Route value**: a blank in a route, in curly braces. What the visitor types there goes into your method.
- **Constraint**: a rule for a route value, like `:int` for whole numbers only.
- **404 Not Found**: the status code that means "there's nothing here".

lessons.title: Routes, route values and query strings
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Routes, route values and query strings

Real APIs are organized around **resources**: books, players, orders. Each has a predictable set of routes, and clients send extra details in the **query string**. Getting these right is what makes an API easy (or painful) to use.

### Route templates and route values

```csharp
app.MapGet("/books/{id:int}", (int id) => …);
app.MapGet("/authors/{name}/books", (string name) => …);
```

`{id:int}` is a **route parameter**. ASP.NET Core matches the request path against each template, pulls out the **route values** and binds them to handler parameters **by name** (case doesn't matter).

### Route constraints

| Constraint | Matches |
|---|---|
| `{id:int}` | whole numbers (`long`, `guid`, `bool`, `decimal` too) |
| `{code:alpha}` | letters only |
| `{n:min(1)}`, `{n:range(1,12)}` | numbers in a range |
| `{slug:minlength(3)}` | text at least that long |
| `{page?}` | optional |

Constraints are about **matching**, not validation. Without `:int`, `GET /books/abc` still matches `/books/{id}`, then binding fails and the client gets **400 Bad Request** with `Failed to bind parameter "int id" from "abc".` With `:int`, the route doesn't match and the answer is **404**. Use constraints to say what a URL *is*, and validation (next lesson) for rules about the data.

When two templates match, the more specific one wins: a literal segment (`/books/new`) beats a constrained parameter (`/books/{id:int}`), which beats a plain one (`/books/{slug}`). Order in the file doesn't matter.

### Query strings

Everything after `?` is the query string: `/books?search=dragon&page=2`. Simple parameters that aren't route values are read from it:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/books", (string? search, int page = 1) => …);
```

- **Required or optional?** A parameter is optional if it's nullable (`string?`, `int?`) or has a default (`int page = 1`). Otherwise a missing value gets **400**: `Required parameter "string search" was not provided from query string.`
- Real projects have **nullable reference types** turned on (`<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` in the project file; `#nullable enable` at the top of a file here), so a plain `string` means *required*.
- Use `[FromQuery(Name = "q")] string? search` when the query name differs from the parameter.

Use route values to **identify** a resource and the query string to **filter, sort or page** a collection.

### Grouping routes

```csharp
var books = app.MapGroup("/books");
books.MapGet("/", …);           // GET /books
books.MapGet("/{id:int}", …);   // GET /books/3
```

### Paging

Returning a whole table is slow and risky, so collections are usually paged. With LINQ:

```csharp
items.Skip((page - 1) * pageSize).Take(pageSize)
```

That's the same idea as `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` in SQL (`OFFSET … FETCH` in SQL Server).

### The null gotcha

```csharp
books.MapGet("/{id:int}", (int id) =>
    list.FirstOrDefault(b => b.Id == id));
```

When the book doesn't exist, `FirstOrDefault` returns `null`, and ASP.NET Core happily answers **200 OK** with the body `null`. Clients then crash trying to read a book that isn't there. Return a real 404:

```csharp
books.MapGet("/{id:int}", (int id) =>
    list.FirstOrDefault(b => b.Id == id) is { } book
        ? Results.Ok(book)
        : Results.NotFound());
```

`is { } book` means "is not null, and call it `book`".

### New words

- **Resource**: a thing your API exposes, like a book or a player, usually at its own route.
- **Route parameter**: a `{name}` placeholder in a route template; its value is a route value.
- **Route constraint**: a rule a route value must meet for the route to match, like `:int`.
- **Query string**: the part of a URL after `?`, made of `name=value` pairs joined by `&`.
- **Paging**: returning a collection one page at a time, with `Skip` and `Take`.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A leaderboard API. `GET /players` takes optional `region` and `top` query values; `GET /players/{id:int}` is a 404 for unknown ids. Press **Run**, then try `GET /players?region=EU`, `GET /players?top=2`, `GET /players/9` and `GET /players/abc` in **Try it**.

challenge.instructionsMarkdown:
**Your turn.** The library app's book API has three problems the app team keeps reporting.

1. **`GET /books/{id}`**: `GET /books/abc` answers 400 and `GET /books/9` answers **200 with `null`**. Both should be **404 Not Found** (and `GET /books/3` still finds *Dragon Rider*).
2. **Search**: `GET /books` with no query string answers 400, because `search` is required. Make it optional, and make it ignore case: `?search=DRAGON` finds both dragon books.
3. **Paging**: answer **2 books per page**. `?page=2` is the second page (books 3 and 4), and no `page` means page 1. Paging works with search too: `?search=dragon&page=2` is an empty list.

The file starts with `#nullable enable`, as real projects do.

lessons.title: Sending data to the server
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Sending data to the server

So far, your servers only **answered** questions. Now visitors will **send** something: a new pet for the Grove pet list!

### POST means "please save this"

To send data, a request uses the method **POST** instead of GET, and carries the data in its **body**, as JSON:

```
POST /pets

{ "name": "Moss", "kind": "frog" }
```

### Reading the body

Use `app.MapPost`, and give your method a parameter whose type matches the JSON:

```csharp
app.MapPost("/pets", (Pet pet) =>
{
    var saved = pet with { Id = pets.Count + 1 };
    pets.Add(saved);
    return Results.Created($"/pets/{saved.Id}", saved);
});
```

- ASP.NET Core turns the JSON body into a `Pet` for you.
- The visitor doesn't choose the id: the server does, with `with { Id = … }`.
- `Results.Created` answers **201 Created**: "it worked, and I saved something new". The first part, `/pets/4`, says where the new pet now lives.

### Saying no

Sometimes the data isn't good enough, like a pet with no name. Then answer **400 Bad Request** and say why:

```csharp
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(pet.Name))
{
    return Results.BadRequest("A pet needs a name.");
}
```

`string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is true for a missing name, an empty one (`""`), or one that's only spaces.

### Try it with a body

In **Try it**, pick **POST**, type the path, and write the JSON in the **Body** box. Then send a GET to see your new pet in the list.

### New words

- **POST**: the request method for sending something new to the server.
- **Request body**: the data a request carries, usually JSON.
- **201 Created**: the status code that means "saved, and here's where it lives".
- **400 Bad Request**: the status code that means "I can't use what you sent".
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A wish list server that accepts new wishes. Press **Run**. In **Try it**, pick **POST**, set the path to `/wishes`, and send the body `{ "text": "a pet dragon" }`. Then `GET /wishes` shows it. Send `{ "text": "" }` too, and see the **400**.

lessons.title: POST, PUT, DELETE and validation
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## POST, PUT, DELETE and validation

Reading data is half an API. The other half is changing it safely: creating, replacing and deleting, while refusing bad input with errors a client can actually use.

### The CRUD endpoints

**CRUD** (create, read, update, delete) maps onto HTTP like this:

| Action | Request | Success answer |
|---|---|---|
| Create | `POST /tasks` + body | **201 Created** + `Location` + the new item |
| Read | `GET /tasks`, `GET /tasks/3` | **200 OK** |
| Replace | `PUT /tasks/3` + body | **204 No Content** (or 200 + the item) |
| Change part | `PATCH /tasks/3` + body | 204 or 200 |
| Delete | `DELETE /tasks/3` | **204 No Content** |

`PUT` and `DELETE` on an id that doesn't exist answer **404**. `PUT` and `DELETE` are **idempotent**: sending the same one twice leaves the same result, so clients can safely retry them. `POST` isn't: twice means two new items.

### Binding the body

A complex parameter (a record or class) is read from the JSON body:

```csharp
app.MapPost("/tasks", (CreateTask input) => …);
```

Names match case-insensitively. Watch out: JSON that leaves a property out gives it its default (`null`, `0`, `false`), **even if the C# type says it can't be null**. Nullable annotations aren't checked at run time, so validate.

### DTOs, and the overposting gotcha

If `POST /tasks` binds your storage type directly:

```csharp
// TaskItem(Id, Title, Points, Done)
app.MapPost("/tasks", (TaskItem task) => …);
```

then any client can send `"id": 99, "done": true` and choose things only the server should decide. That's **overposting**. Instead, bind a **DTO** (*data transfer object*) with only the fields a client may set:

```csharp
record CreateTask(string Title, int Points);
```

and build the stored item yourself: `new TaskItem(nextId++, input.Title, input.Points, false)`.

### Validation and problem details

Clients need to know **which field** is wrong. `Results.ValidationProblem` sends a 400 in the standard problem details format with an `errors` object:

```csharp
var errors = new Dictionary<string, string[]>();
if (input.Points is < 1 or > 13)
    errors["points"] = ["Points must be from 1 to 13."];
if (errors.Count > 0)
    return Results.ValidationProblem(errors);
```

```json
{
  "title": "One or more validation errors occurred.",
  "status": 400,
  "errors": { "points": ["Points must be from 1 to 13."] }
}
```

Use the JSON names (camelCase) as keys, so the client can show each message next to its field.

In .NET 10, `builder.Services.AddValidation()` can do this for you from attributes like `[Required]` and `[Range(1, 13)]`. It's worth knowing exactly what it does first, so this lesson writes the checks by hand. (Codegrove's practice server doesn't support `AddValidation()` yet.)

### Replace and delete

```csharp
app.MapDelete("/tasks/{id:int}", (int id) =>
    tasks.RemoveAll(t => t.Id == id) > 0
        ? Results.NoContent()
        : Results.NotFound());
```

Records are immutable, so `PUT` replaces the item: find its index with `FindIndex`, then `tasks[index] = new TaskItem(…)`.

### New words

- **CRUD**: create, read, update, delete: the four things most APIs do to data.
- **DTO** (*data transfer object*): a type shaped for what goes over the wire, not for how it's stored.
- **Overposting**: a client setting fields it shouldn't, because the endpoint bound too much.
- **Idempotent**: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once (`PUT`, `DELETE`, `GET`).
- **Validation**: checking incoming data against your rules before using it.
- **204 No Content**: success with no body.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A notes API with create and delete. `POST /notes` binds a `CreateNote` DTO and answers a validation problem for blank text. Press **Run**, then in **Try it**: POST `/notes` with `{ "text": "Practice scales" }`, POST `{ "text": " " }` (look at the `errors` object), then `DELETE /notes/1` twice: 204, then 404.

lessons.title: Helpers the server can ask for
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Helpers the server can ask for

Your servers kept their lists right in `Program.cs`. As a server grows, that gets messy. Real servers put each job in its own class, called a **service**, and let ASP.NET Core hand it to any endpoint that needs it.

### A service is just a class

`PetBook` keeps the Grove's pets and knows how to find them:

```csharp
class PetBook
{
    private readonly List<Pet> _pets = [new("Pip", "owl")];

    public List<Pet> All() => _pets;
    public Pet? Find(string name) =>
        _pets.FirstOrDefault(p => p.Name == name);
}
```

### Step 1: tell the app about it

Before `builder.Build()`, **register** the service:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddSingleton<PetBook>();
```

**Singleton** means the app makes **one** `PetBook` and shares it with every request, so pets added by one visitor are there for the next.

### Step 2: ask for it

Any endpoint can now ask for a `PetBook` just by having a parameter of that type:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/pets", (PetBook book) => book.All());
```

You never write `new PetBook()`. ASP.NET Core sees the parameter and passes in the shared one. This is called **dependency injection**: the things your code depends on are handed (injected) to it.

### Forgot to register it?

ASP.NET Core doesn't know `PetBook` is a service, so it thinks the visitor is meant to *send* a PetBook in the request body. A GET request has no body, so the endpoint can't run at all: the answer is **500**, and the Output panel says to register `PetBook`. That's your clue to add `AddSingleton`.

### New words

- **Service**: a class that does one job for the server, like keeping the pet list.
- **Register**: telling the app about a service with `builder.Services.Add…`.
- **Singleton**: one shared copy of a service for the whole app.
- **Dependency injection**: the app hands each endpoint the services it asks for.

Because there's one shared `PetBook`, a pet you POST (try `{ "name": "Moss", "kind": "frog" }`) is still there for the next request: `GET /pets/count` says **4**.

lessons.title: Services and dependency injection
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Services and dependency injection

Endpoints that do everything themselves (store data, apply rules, read the time) are hard to change and almost impossible to test. ASP.NET Core is built around **dependency injection** (DI): classes declare what they need in their constructor, and a **container** creates them and passes those needs in.

### Register, then inject

```csharp
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IScoreStore, InMemoryScoreStore>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<ScoreService>();
var app = builder.Build();

app.MapGet("/top", (ScoreService scores) => scores.Top(3));
```

- `AddSingleton<IScoreStore, InMemoryScoreStore>()`: "when someone asks for an `IScoreStore`, give them an `InMemoryScoreStore`." Code depends on the **interface**, so you can swap in a database-backed store later without touching it.
- `ScoreService` asks for an `IScoreStore` in its constructor; the container supplies it. Handlers ask for services as parameters.
- Every registration must happen **before** `builder.Build()`.

### Lifetimes

| Lifetime | One instance per… | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Singleton** | the whole app | in-memory caches and stores, clocks, configuration |
| **Scoped** | HTTP request | a database context (`DbContext`), per-request state |
| **Transient** | every time it's asked for | small, stateless helpers |

Inside one request, every class that asks for a scoped service gets **the same** instance. The next request gets a new one.

### The captive dependency gotcha

A singleton lives for the whole app. If it holds a scoped service, that service gets **captured** and reused across requests, which breaks things like a `DbContext`. In Development, ASP.NET Core checks every registration at `Build()` and refuses to start:

```
Cannot consume scoped service 'RequestLog'
from singleton 'ScoreService'.
```

The fix is to give the consumer a lifetime **no longer** than its dependencies: make `ScoreService` scoped, or make what it holds a singleton if it's really app-wide.

The opposite mistake is quieter: register an in-memory store as **scoped**, and each request gets a fresh, empty store. Data "disappears" between requests, with no error.

### Inject what changes, too

```csharp
public class ScoreService(IScoreStore store, IClock clock) { … }
```

Even `DateTime.UtcNow` is a dependency. Hide it behind an `IClock`, register `SystemClock` for the real app, and tests can pass a `FixedClock` to check time-dependent rules exactly. (.NET has a built-in `TimeProvider` for this; here we write the interface ourselves.)

The `(IScoreStore store, IClock clock)` after the class name is a **primary constructor**: its parameters are available throughout the class.

### New words

- **Dependency injection** (DI): classes receive what they depend on instead of creating it.
- **DI container**: the part of ASP.NET Core that creates services and passes in their dependencies (`builder.Services`).
- **Service lifetime**: how long one instance lives: singleton, scoped or transient.
- **Captive dependency**: a longer-lived service holding a shorter-lived one, like a singleton holding a scoped service.
- **Primary constructor**: constructor parameters written after the class name.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: Three lifetimes side by side. `IGreeting` is resolved to `FriendlyGreeting`; the two `RequestCounter` parameters are the same scoped instance within a request; `VisitCounter` is a singleton, so `visit` keeps counting. Give `ScoreService` a lifetime that fits.
2. **Scores must stick.** Every saved score has to stay in the store as long as the app runs, so `GET /scores/top` lists scores from earlier requests. Choose the store's lifetime with that in mind.
3. **Inject the clock.** `ScoreService` makes its own `SystemClock`, so tests can't control the time.
